title: The Psychology of Home Environments: A Call for Research on Residential Space
central_proposition: Homes are consequential real-world settings that provide a rich and informative context for studying a wide variety of fundamental psychological processes, yet they are largely neglected in empirical psychological research.

concept_definitions.name: Home
concept_definitions.definition: A unique place where a person's past, present, and future selves are reflected and come to life, distinguished from a mere residence by qualities such as community, privacy, self-expression, personal identity, and warmth.

concept_definitions.name: Ambiance
concept_definitions.definition: The important emotions or perceptions individuals desire to evoke within themselves and others in a specific physical space.

concept_definitions.name: Emotion Regulation (via physical spaces)
concept_definitions.definition: The process by which individuals select and modify their physical environments (e.g., organization, decor, ambient features) to initiate, avoid, maintain, reduce, or enhance core emotional states.

argument_structure: The paper first establishes the societal and personal importance of homes, then highlights their neglect in empirical psychology. It synthesizes existing theoretical and limited empirical insights from various disciplines that hint at the psychological significance of homes. It then proposes specific areas within psychology (e.g., emotion regulation, identity, development) where homes offer rich research contexts. An exploratory study on desired home ambiances is presented to illustrate the potential insights. Finally, the paper connects these findings to broader psychological theories and advocates for interdisciplinary collaboration.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Homes influence psychological processes through several mechanisms: they serve as reconstructions of past safe spaces, influencing feelings of security; their physical features (layout, ambient conditions) constrain or promote specific activities and social interactions, which in turn affect cognitive and emotional states; items and arrangements within homes convey impressions and identity; mementos and personal artifacts evoke memories and provide social support; and physical spaces, being both flexible and stable, act as pervasive and precise mechanisms for emotion regulation across multiple sensory channels (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, ambient, social). This person-environment interaction is driven by individuals selecting and manipulating spaces to match their personalities, goals, and values.

findings.antecedent: Individuals' home environments (as reconstructions of past safe spaces)
findings.mechanism: Unconscious incorporation of features from well-loved past spaces that were associated with safety and security.
findings.quote: individuals' home environments are reconstructions of past spaces in which those people felt safe and secure.

findings.antecedent: Physical features of a space (e.g., layout, ambient features like lighting levels, temperature, humidity, noise, music, color, shape)
findings.consequent: Activities performed, social interactions, occupant's mood, concentration, and productivity
findings.mechanism: Physical features are suited to specific activities; layout influences interactions; ambient features directly affect cognitive and emotional states.
findings.quote: features of a space can influence the activities likely to be performed in that space... which in turn may affect cognitive and emotional states
findings.empirical_support_cited: Gao et al. (2007), Gifford (2007), Jasnoski (1992), Küller et al. (2006), Boubekri et al. (1991)

findings.antecedent: Items in a space and their arrangement (e.g., photos of relatives, political symbols, cultural artifacts)
findings.consequent: Impressions conveyed to others, importance placed on family, political orientation, well-being, feelings of social support, loneliness, social isolation
findings.mechanism: Items serve as symbols or 'social snacks' that communicate identity, values, or provide tangible reminders of connections.
findings.quote: the items in a space and their arrangement can be used to convey impressions to others
findings.empirical_support_cited: Carney et al. (2008), Gifford (2007), Gardner et al. (2005)

findings.mechanism: Mementos act as cues for memory retrieval, linking current space to past experiences and people.
findings.quote: mementos may evoke fond memories of other times, places, and people.

findings.mechanism: The physical layout can constrain or facilitate behaviors and interactions that influence physiological stress responses and emotional states.
findings.quote: the physical layout of a space can affect daily mood and cortisol levels

findings.antecedent: Life stressors outside the home (e.g., job stress)
findings.mechanism: Stressors from external domains can spill over into the home environment, influencing domestic interactions and activities.
findings.quote: life stressors that occur outside of the home (e.g., job stress) can affect behaviors within the home
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ilies et al. (2007), Judge & Ilies (2004), Repetti et al. (2009), Saxbe & Repetti (2008), Wang & Repetti (2013), Wang et al. (2011)

findings.consequent: Children's cognitive and academic performance, health risks, exposure to environmental toxins/disease, negative emotion in infants, disruptive behaviors
findings.mechanism: Environmental disorganization and density create stress and cognitive load, impairing development and well-being.
findings.quote: children living in chaotic, crowded homes tend to perform less effectively cognitively and academically
findings.empirical_support_cited: Evans et al. (2005), Goux & Maurin (2005), Hanscombe et al. (2011), Baker et al. (1998), Leventhal & Newman (2010), Mann et al. (1992), Bridgett et al. (2013), Jaffee et al. (2012)

findings.antecedent: Residential mobility (frequency of moving to a new home)
findings.consequent: Academic performance, emotional and social issues, psychological values, early mortality
findings.mechanism: Frequent changes in environment disrupt social networks, educational continuity, and sense of place, leading to various negative outcomes.
findings.quote: residential mobility... has been tied to a broad range of outcomes, including academic performance, emotional and social issues
findings.empirical_support_cited: Leventhal & Newman (2010), Flouri (2009), Oishi (2010), Oishi & Schimmack (2010)

findings.antecedent: Physical spaces (characterized by flexibility and stability)
findings.mechanism: Spaces can be organized, decorated, and furnished in many ways (flexibility) and exert persistent, predictable effects (stability), allowing for fine-tuned emotional regulation through multiple sensory channels (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, ambient, social).
findings.source: Connecting home psychology to the broader field
findings.quote: physical spaces may be a particularly pervasive and powerful mechanism for regulating emotions because spaces are flexible and stable.

findings.antecedent: Individuals' personalities, goals, attitudes, and values
findings.consequent: Selection, manipulation, and evocation of physical spaces (including homes)
findings.mechanism: People actively shape their environments to match their internal states and preferences, reflecting a person-environment fit.
findings.source: Connecting home psychology to the broader field
findings.quote: Interactionist approaches in environmental and personality research emphasize the role of individuals in selecting, manipulating, and evoking situations and environments to match their personalities, goals, attitudes, and values

findings.antecedent: Desired ambiances in ideal home spaces (e.g., inviting, organization, relaxation, restoration, kinship, storage, stimulation, intimacy, productivity)
findings.consequent: Specific ambiances desired, systematic variation across rooms, six broad ambiance dimensions
findings.mechanism: People have shared preferences for emotional and perceptual states in different home spaces, reflecting their functional and psychological roles. PCA revealed underlying dimensions.
findings.source: Mapping Desired Psychological Ambiances in the Home: An Illustrative Study
findings.quote: individuals desire a broad range of specific ambiances in their ideal living spaces. ... The ambiances also differed systematically across spaces.

findings.antecedent: Room type (e.g., entryway, kitchen, bedroom, garage)
findings.mechanism: Different rooms serve distinct practical and social functions, leading to specific desired psychological ambiances for each.
findings.source: Mapping Desired Psychological Ambiances in the Home: An Illustrative Study
findings.quote: The ambiances also differed systematically across spaces. For example, many participants wanted a romantic bedroom, but none of them wanted a romantic garage.

findings.consequent: Psychological states experienced in a space, activities occurring within the space
findings.mechanism: Physical features directly or indirectly shape how people feel and what they do in a space, informing how spaces can be designed to achieve desired outcomes.
findings.source: Stepping outside the home: A broader psychology of physical spaces
findings.quote: a fuller understanding of how physical features influence the psychological states experienced in a space and the activities that occur within the space can inform how spaces are designed to help achieve a desired outcome.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Home spaces reflect relationship dynamics and home design influences interpersonal processes, which in turn affect the development and longevity of romantic relationships.
The layout of a space interferes with or promotes couples' individual needs for intimacy and independence.
Couples' choice of decor reflects status and role dynamics in their relationship.
Whether Person A moves into Person B's home or they start afresh with a new one matters to a cohabiting relationship.
People shape their domestic spaces to facilitate avenues of emotional expression (e.g., sharing gossip on the porch) or as a means of escape (e.g., disappearing into a 'man cave').
The home facilitates the consumption of emotion-regulating entertainment (e.g., music, television, art, literature).
Home spaces are used in the service of identity negotiation, and physical characteristics of a person's space provide a barometer of their ongoing process of identity development.
Longitudinal and cross-sectional studies can reveal markers of psychological transitions (e.g., puberty, living alone, marriage, divorce, having children) in home environments.
The design and decoration of spaces reflect conceptions of privacy and the practice of gender segregation in different cultures (e.g., Qatari homes).
The ambiances people want to elicit vary systematically across different areas of a home.
People's self-reported desired ambiances for ideal homes reflect their actual behaviors in their own spaces, rather than naive theories.
The extent to which desired ambiances are directed to the occupants themselves versus visitors varies across public and private spaces.
Desired ambiances are affected by factors such as income, gender, culture, age, class, ownership status (owned/rented), and living arrangements (alone/with others).
Specific variables (e.g., personality traits) determine preferences for evoking particular ambiances (e.g., abundance vs. togetherness in a kitchen).
bridge_warrants: The paper connects environmental psychology's interactionist perspectives with emotion regulation theories, arguing that physical spaces are a powerful, yet overlooked, mechanism for regulating emotions.

It bridges psychology with architecture, design, and engineering by proposing that psychological insights into how people perceive and use spaces can inform the design of environments that facilitate desired functions (e.g., healing in hospitals, healthy living, cognitive support for dementia patients).
It links sociology's focus on broad social factors (gender, race, class) to psychology by suggesting that the mechanisms of their influence often play out in domestic contexts.
It connects legal theories regarding property rights and 'personhood' to psychological justifications, highlighting the psychological significance of home ownership and control.
methodological_critiques: Contemporary research on emotion and emotion regulation has largely ignored the topic of physical space, with relevant terms often absent from handbooks and keyword searches.

Past work on home environments primarily used direct-observation, daily telephone interviewing, and daily diary methods, which can be intrusive; new technologies (e.g., automatic sensing from smartphones) hold promise for reduced intrusiveness and greater fidelity.
model_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual framework where homes serve as a nexus for various psychological processes (e.g., identity, emotion regulation, social interaction, development) influenced by physical features (layout, decor, ambient conditions) and broader factors (mobility, culture). This framework emphasizes the active role of individuals in selecting and manipulating their environments to achieve desired psychological states, and it highlights the home's unique properties (flexibility, stability) as an ideal context for studying these processes.
limitations: The exploratory study is preliminary and survey-based, focusing on 'ideal homes' rather than actual behaviors, which may reflect naive theories rather than real-world actions.
The study did not differentiate between ambiances desired for occupants themselves versus visitors.
The exploratory study did not examine how desired ambiances are affected by factors such as income, gender, culture, age, class, ownership status, or living arrangements.

paper_metadata.title: The Psychology of Home Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Homes are important: People devote much of their thought, time, and resources to selecting, modifying, and decorating their living spaces, and they may be devastated when their homes must be sold or are destroyed. Yet the empirical psychological literature says virtually nothing about the roles that homes might play in people’s lives. We argue that homes provide an informative context for a wide variety of studies examining how social, developmental, cognitive, and other psychological processes play out in a consequential real-world setting. The topic of homes is also well suited to collaborations with a diverse array of disciplines ranging from architecture and engineering to sociology and law. We illustrate the potential insights to be gained from studying homes with an exploratory study that maps the psychological ambiances (e.g., romance, comfort, togetherness) that people desire in their homes; we identify six broad ambiance dimensions (restoration, kinship, storage, stimulation, intimacy, productivity) that show mean differences across rooms. We connect these findings to existing work on situation selection in emotion regulation. These ideas provide only an initial foray into the domain of residential space, but they hint at the productive roles that homes and other spaces could play in psychological theorizing and research.
